paras: The killing of Governor Harper was the death of a Black road hand, Governor Harper, struck on the head with a hoe by a white man, David Lewis, during a quarrel near Ruckersville, Georgia, in early August 1881. Lewis was arrested, and a crowd of Black men then tried to take him from his guard to lynch him.
According to the Anderson Intelligencer, the two men had gathered with others at the Goss place, two miles from Ruckersville, to work the roads.

There Lewis accused Harper of stealing fruit from a Mrs. Goss, and Harper, denying it, invited Lewis to settle the matter in a fight. By the Intelligencer's account, Harper picked up a rock and Lewis struck him with a hoe about 9 a.m.; he never spoke again and died about 1 p.m.

Those present arrested Lewis. While he was under guard, a crowd of Black men tried to seize him to lynch him, and the Elberton Gazette said a guard fired small shot into the crowd. The crowd followed the guard and prisoner to a nearby house, Mrs. Cleveland's in the Intelligencer, until threats dispersed it.
No report of an inquest or a trial of Lewis appears in the coverage.

The Savannah Morning News ran the Gazette item on August 13 among its "Georgia Affairs" briefs, and the Marietta Journal reprinted it on August 18. That text called the encounter a "difficulty" between "Mr. David Lewis and a negro named Governor," giving the dead man no surname. The Anderson Intelligencer of South Carolina printed a fuller paragraph the same day naming "a colored man named Governor Harper." None of the papers commented on the killing or on the attempted lynching.

The Gazette said Harper "died immediately," while the Intelligencer, which named the attending physician, said he lived about four hours. Only the Intelligencer mentioned the rock, and its "Wednesday of last week" in an August 18 issue does not fix the date, since Savannah had the story by August 13.

reader.title: Killing of Governor Harper
bases: A single white man, David Lewis, killed Harper with a hoe in a quarrel among a road-working crew (A2, A3, A4); no mob, band or officers took part in the killing, and the attempted lynching that followed was by a Black crowd against Lewis, a separate episode.

The Elberton Gazette brief (A2, A4) and the Anderson Intelligencer's longer and evidently separately sourced account (A3) agree that Lewis struck Harper with a hoe and that he died, though A2 and A4 share one text.

accounts.label: Elberton Gazette brief
accounts.gist: During a 'difficulty' on a road crew, Lewis struck Governor with the eye of a hoe and he died immediately; a crowd of Black men tried to lynch Lewis and was driven off with small shot and threats.

accounts.label: Anderson Intelligencer account
accounts.gist: Lewis accused Harper of stealing fruit; Harper invited him to fight and picked up a rock, and Lewis hit him with a hoe; Harper died four hours later; the crowd that tried to lynch Lewis followed the guard to Mrs. Cleveland's house.

framing.detail: Georgia briefs columns ('Georgia Affairs', 'Georgia Gleanings') relay the Gazette's 'difficulty' between 'Mr. David Lewis and a negro named Governor' without comment.
The Anderson Intelligencer's paragraph names both men by race and full name and gives the quarrel in detail, including Harper's rock, without comment.
